blocks.title: Meaning and origins
blocks.md: **Pan-Africanism** is the idea that people of African descent share a common history and interests and should unite to defend their rights and, later, to free and unite Africa. It began in the African diaspora, notably in the USA and the Caribbean, in the late 19th century. The first Pan-African Conference met in London in **1900**, organised with the help of Henry Sylvester Williams.

blocks.title: Congresses and figures
blocks.md: W. E. B. Du Bois led a series of Pan-African Congresses from **1919**. Marcus Garvey promoted racial pride. The Fifth Congress in **Manchester in 1945**, with George Padmore, Kwame Nkrumah and others, called for an end to colonial rule and marked a turn towards African leadership. Related currents: **Négritude** (cultural pride, Senghor, Césaire) and Nkrumah’s call for a ‘United States of Africa’.

blocks.caption: Pan-Africanism from 1900 to the AU.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1895 to 2005 with the London conference 1900, Manchester 1945, OAU founded 1963 and AU launched 2002.

blocks.title: Disagreement on unity
blocks.md: After independence, African leaders disagreed. The **Casablanca group** (1961), including Ghana, wanted rapid political union. The **Monrovia group** preferred cooperation among sovereign states. A compromise at Addis Ababa in 1963 created the Organisation of African Unity, favouring cooperation rather than a federation.

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- Pan-Africanism began among people of African descent abroad, not only in Africa.
- Pan-Africanism and the OAU are linked but not the same.
- Leaders differed: unity could mean a political union or looser cooperation.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Manchester 1945
blocks.statement: Explain the importance of the 1945 Manchester Pan-African Congress.
steps: It demanded an end to colonial rule at a time when many colonies were changing.
African leaders such as Nkrumah took a leading role.
It linked Pan-Africanism to the nationalist movements that won independence.
blocks.answer: It turned Pan-Africanism towards independence led by Africans.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Two approaches
blocks.statement: Contrast the Casablanca and Monrovia groups.
steps: Casablanca: rapid political union under strong central authority.
Monrovia: gradual cooperation among independent states, with respect for sovereignty.
The OAU combined elements, favouring the Monrovia approach.

blocks.title: The OAU
blocks.md: The **Organisation of African Unity (OAU)** was founded at Addis Ababa on **25 May 1963** by thirty-two independent African states. Aims: promote unity and solidarity, defend sovereignty and territorial integrity, end colonialism and apartheid, and promote cooperation. Principles: sovereign equality, **non-interference** in internal affairs and peaceful settlement of disputes. A 1964 resolution accepted inherited colonial borders.

blocks.title: Record of the OAU
blocks.md: **Achievements:** supported liberation movements through its Liberation Committee, helped end colonial rule in southern Africa, mediated some disputes and gave Africa a voice at the UN. **Weaknesses:** no power to enforce, the principle of non-interference limited action against abuses and civil wars, lack of money, divisions among members.

blocks.caption: OAU and AU compared.
blocks.alt: A table comparing foundation date, headquarters and main principle of the OAU and the AU.

blocks.title: The AU
blocks.md: The **African Union (AU)** replaced the OAU, launched in **2002** (the Constitutive Act was adopted in 2000). It has a stronger structure: an Assembly of heads of state, a Commission, the **Peace and Security Council**, and the Pan-African Parliament. It allows intervention in member states in grave circumstances such as genocide and war crimes. It also promotes development through programmes such as NEPAD and **Agenda 2063**.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.md:
- The OAU did not accept the right to interfere in members’ internal affairs; the AU’s Act recognises a limited right of intervention.
- Headquarters are in Addis Ababa (Ethiopia) for both.
- Do not state the AU’s success or failure without evidence: assess both.

blocks.title: Example 1 — OAU versus AU
blocks.statement: State two differences between the OAU and the AU.
steps: The AU has a Peace and Security Council and a Pan-African Parliament; the OAU had no such bodies.
The AU’s Act permits intervention in grave circumstances; the OAU stressed non-interference.
blocks.answer: Stronger institutions and a limited right of intervention.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why accept colonial borders?
blocks.statement: Why did the OAU accept the borders inherited from colonial rule?
steps: Changing borders could cause many disputes and wars.
New states wanted stability and recognition of their territory.
It avoided arguments over which groups should belong to which state.
blocks.answer: To avoid conflict and protect stability.

objectives: Describe political, economic and social challenges after independence
Explain the causes of instability and conflict
reviewNotes: Verify general claims about coups and one-party states in the 1960s–80s and the 1990s democratisation; avoid listing countries unless sure of facts.

blocks.title: Political challenges
blocks.md: New states had borders from colonial times, many ethnic and language groups and weak national institutions. **Nation-building** meant creating a common identity. In many countries early multiparty systems gave way to **one-party states** and **military coups** in the 1960s–80s; in the 1990s many states returned to multiparty politics. Conflicts and weak governance harmed development.

blocks.title: Economic and social challenges
blocks.md: Economies depended on **exporting a few primary products**, so falling world prices hurt incomes. Colonial infrastructure linked mines and farms to ports, not to each other. Debt, poverty, limited industry, rapid population growth, shortages in education, health and skilled workers, and disease posed further problems. Some argue that external economic influence continued (**neo-colonialism**); others stress internal factors.

blocks.caption: Common challenges after independence.
blocks.alt: Six boxes listing institutions, divisions, export dependence, debt, conflict and education and health.

blocks.title: Responses and progress
blocks.md: Governments expanded schools and health services, built roads and dams, and set up regional organisations. Since the 1990s many states have held multiparty elections and economic reforms. The AU and regional communities try to manage conflict and promote trade. Progress is uneven: some countries have grown steadily, while others face conflict and poverty.

blocks.title: Write with balance
blocks.md:
- Avoid blaming only colonialism or only African leaders: weigh both internal and external factors.
- Do not treat Africa as uniform: experiences differ widely.
- Present contested political questions neutrally and attribute opinions.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Internal or external?
blocks.statement: Classify as internal or external: (a) weak institutions, (b) falling cocoa prices on the world market, (c) a coup, (d) debt owed to foreign lenders.
steps: Many problems combine both kinds of causes.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why diversify?
blocks.statement: Explain why dependence on one export is risky for a new state.
steps: World prices vary, so income falls when prices fall.
Little industry means few jobs and little added value.
Diversification and processing spread the risk.

exercises.prompt: Assess the view that the main cause of Africa’s post-independence problems was the legacy of colonial rule.
exercises.model: Colonial rule left artificial borders, economies built around exports, little investment in education and weak institutions, which made later problems more severe. But decisions after independence, such as governance, corruption, conflict and policy choices, and outside factors like prices and debt, also mattered. The legacy was important but was not the only cause, and the balance varies from country to country.
